To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the synovial fluids of patients with inflammatory and degenerative joint diseases have elevated levels of lysosomal enzymes compared to those of normal individuals.

the synovial fluids obtained from patients with rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis have increased concentrations of intracellular enzymes and that the concentrations of these enzymes correlate with the concentrations of lysosomal enzymes.

the synovial fluids of patients with inflammatory and non-inflammatory joint diseases differ in their composition of lysosomal enzymes and that these changes are accompanied by the release into the joint space of other intracellular proteins.

the study of enzymes released into synovial fluid from the joint tissue and the cells of synovial lining in various joint diseases.

the presence of enzymes of intracellular origin in the synovium is the result of the presence of a disease, and that the enzymes of intracellular organelles are not specific to any of the diseases.
the synovial fluids of the inflammatory and non-inflammatory joint diseases studied have a different composition of enzymes.
the synovial fluids from the different rheumatic diseases are not characterized by any particular enzyme profile, but that the presence of intracellular enzymes is a common phenomenon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lysosomal enzymes, as well as the other intracellular enzymes, are released in the synovia from the damaged cells.

, in the inflammatory joint disease, the release of enzymes into synovial fluid seems to be the result of an increased cell permeability, and that this increase is probably the result of an altered permeability of the cell membrane rather than of a change in the lysosomal membrane.
the lysosomal enzymes are released into the synovial fluids in rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis in the same manner as the non-lysosomal enzymes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have demonstrated that lysosomal enzyme release in the synovium is a non-specific phenomenon, and that the presence of these enzymes does not necessarily reflect the presence of inflammation.
the release of lysosomes is not specific for any disease and that the presence of intracellular enzymes in synovia is the result of cell death or of an overall change of the membrane permeability.
